subject: Samhällskunskap
title: Democracy and influence
sourceSummary: What democracy means in practice — majority decisions and protection for minorities, how you can have influence at school and in society, what distinguishes democracy from dictatorship, and what universal suffrage means.
topics: having influence at school and in society

questions.prompt: The word democracy comes from Greek. What does it literally mean?
questions.opener: The word has two parts: one meaning people and one meaning power.
choices: Rule by a king
Rule by the military
Rule by the people
Rule by judges
questions.explanation: Democracy comes from demos (people) and kratos (power or rule) and thus means rule by the people — power comes from the people. Rule by a king and rule by the military are instead examples of a single person or a small group holding power.

questions.prompt: What is meant by a majority decision?
questions.opener: Think about what you do in class when you vote on something.
choices: The proposal that gets the most votes wins
Everyone must be in complete agreement before the decision is valid
Whoever speaks loudest gets to decide
The teacher chooses among the proposals after the vote
questions.explanation: A majority decision means that the proposal that gets the most votes is the one that stands. Everyone having to agree is instead called consensus, and that is a different way of deciding that often takes much longer.

questions.prompt: Why is protection for minorities needed in a democracy?
questions.opener: Think about what happens to the person who voted for the proposal that lost.
choices: So that the minority always gets to decide instead
So that voting goes faster
So that the minority doesn't have to follow the laws
So that basic rights apply even to those who voted in the minority — the majority is not allowed to vote away others' human rights
questions.explanation: Democracy is more than counting votes: rights such as freedom of speech, freedom of religion and the right not to be discriminated against apply to everyone, even the person who lost the vote. Minority protection does not, however, mean that the minority gets to decide instead or is exempt from following the laws.

questions.topic: having influence at school and in society
questions.opener: The name reveals who sits on it — but who chose them?
choices: A group of teachers who decide the students' timetables
Students chosen by their classes to bring the students' views to the school
The head teacher's own leadership team
A group of parents who review the school
questions.explanation: The student council consists of students whom the classes themselves have chosen, and it is one of the most common ways for students to influence their school. The head teacher's leadership team and parent cooperation also exist, but they are not the student council.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is typical of a dictatorship but not of a democracy?
questions.opener: Think about whether citizens can replace those in power, and whether the media are allowed to scrutinise them.
choices: Regular free elections where several parties are allowed to stand
Courts that are independent of those in power
The right to demonstrate against the government
That the media are controlled by those in power and that criticism of the leadership can be punished
questions.explanation: In a dictatorship, those in power often control the media and criticism can lead to punishment, while free elections and independent courts are absent. Free elections, independent courts and the right to demonstrate are precisely what characterises a democracy.

questions.opener: The word universal means the right is not limited to a particular group.
choices: That only those who pay a lot of tax are allowed to vote
That all adult citizens have the right to vote, regardless of gender, income or background
That you must vote or you get fined
That you can vote as many times as you like
questions.explanation: Universal suffrage means that the right to vote applies to all adult citizens and is not linked to gender, income or social class. In Sweden, universal and equal suffrage for women and men was decided in 1919 and 1921, and it was used for the first time in the parliamentary election of 1921. Voting is a right, not a duty, so it is voluntary.

questions.topic: having influence at school and in society
questions.prompt: You and your classmates think the schoolyard needs more seating. Describe step by step how you can go about influencing this in a democratic way.
questions.opener: Start in your own classroom and work your way up through the school's decision-making channels.
questions.answer: You start by formulating the proposal clearly: more seating in the schoolyard, and why it's needed. Then you raise it at the class council so the whole class can discuss and vote on the proposal. The class representative brings the proposal to the student council, where all classes take part and can support it. The student council passes the proposal on to the head teacher or the school's leadership, who make the decision and may need to take money and safety into account. If you're turned down, you can ask why, come back with a cheaper proposal, or turn to the municipality, which owns many schools.
steps: Formulate the proposal briefly and concretely, and write down the reasons why it's needed.
Raise the proposal at the class council and vote — that shows that more than one person supports it.
The class representative takes the proposal further to the student council, where all classes are represented.
The student council passes the proposal to the head teacher or school leadership, who decide and take budget and safety into account.
If you're turned down: ask for the reasons, adjust the proposal, or turn to the municipality, which is responsible for the school's premises.

questions.prompt: Summarise the most important points about democracy, influence and the right to vote.
questions.opener: Take the meaning of democracy first, then ways of deciding, ways to have influence, and the opposite, dictatorship.
questions.answer: Democracy: from the Greek demos (people) and kratos (power) — rule by the people, power comes from the people · Direct democracy: everyone votes themselves on every issue, e.g. a class council or a referendum · Representative democracy: the people elect representatives who decide, e.g. parliament and the municipal council · Majority decision: the proposal with the most votes wins · Minority protection: rights such as freedom of speech and freedom of religion apply to everyone, even those who voted in the minority · Having influence at school: class council, student council, talking with the head teacher · Having influence in society: voting, joining a party or association, writing a letter to the editor, demonstrating, starting a petition · Democracy is characterised by free elections, several parties, freedom of speech, free media and independent courts · Dictatorship: power cannot be replaced in free elections, the media are controlled and criticism can be punished · Universal suffrage: all adult citizens can vote regardless of gender, income or background — in Sweden from the 1921 election · Voting age in Sweden today: 18.

questions.opener: Think about who votes — the people themselves or chosen representatives?
choices: When the people themselves vote directly on every issue, for example in a referendum
When a king decides everything
When only politicians are allowed to vote
When no one is allowed to vote
questions.explanation: Direct democracy means that citizens themselves vote on every individual issue, for example in a referendum or a class council. It differs from representative democracy, where the people instead elect representatives who then make the decisions on their behalf.

questions.opener: Think about how parliamentary elections work in Sweden.
choices: The people elect representatives, such as members of parliament, who then make the decisions
Everyone votes on every single issue
One person decides without any election
Only companies are allowed to vote
questions.explanation: In a representative democracy, the people elect representatives, such as members of parliament, who then make decisions on their behalf. It is the most common form of democracy in larger countries, since it isn't practically possible for everyone to vote on every single issue.

questions.prompt: In a class of 30 students, 18 vote for a trip to the forest and 12 vote for a trip to town. Which proposal wins according to the majority principle?
questions.opener: Compare how many voted for each proposal.
choices: Town, because the votes there should count double
The forest, because most people voted for it
Neither, because it wasn't unanimous
The teacher decides regardless of the votes
questions.explanation: 18 out of 30 votes is a majority, so the forest wins according to the majority principle. A majority decision doesn't require everyone to agree, only that the proposal gets the most votes.

questions.opener: Think about whether citizens can replace those who govern.
choices: That power can be replaced through free elections
That one person holds power forever without any election
That the media are controlled by the state
That criticism of the leadership is forbidden
questions.explanation: A democracy is characterised by citizens being able to replace those in power through free and regular elections. Power staying in place forever without elections, the media being controlled, and criticism being forbidden are instead characteristics of a dictatorship.

questions.topic: having influence at school and in society
questions.prompt: What is one way to have influence in society outside of school?
questions.opener: Think about the democratic channels available to adult citizens.
choices: Voting in an election, joining a party, or writing a letter to the editor
Waiting for someone else to solve the problem
Only complaining to yourself at home
It isn't possible to have influence as a private individual
questions.explanation: Voting, joining a party or an association, writing a letter to the editor, demonstrating, or starting a petition are all ways to have influence in society. As a private individual there are therefore several democratic channels you can use, even between elections.

questions.prompt: In which year was universal and equal suffrage for women and men used for the first time in a Swedish parliamentary election?
questions.opener: The decision was made in 1919 and 1921 — but when was the first election held under the new suffrage rules?
questions.explanation: Universal and equal suffrage for women and men was decided in 1919 and 1921, but was used for the first time in the parliamentary election of 1921. That is why 1921 is usually counted as the year Sweden achieved universal suffrage in practice.

questions.prompt: What does it mean that citizens have basic freedoms and rights in a democracy?
questions.opener: Think about what would happen if only some people were allowed to express their opinions freely.
choices: That citizens have the right to, among other things, freedom of speech, freedom of assembly and a fair trial
That only some citizens have rights
That rights only apply to adults over the age of 65
That rights can be taken away by anyone
questions.explanation: In a democracy, all citizens have basic freedoms and rights, for example freedom of speech, freedom of assembly and the right to a fair trial. They apply equally to all citizens, not just a particular group, and cannot be arbitrarily removed by individuals or even by the majority.
